findings.premise: Session mapping, idle release and semaphore-based store protection implement the upstream stakeholder decisions.
findings.evidence: DEF resolved questions q0f4e77ae and q2f95abad explicitly select a session-keyed pool released on idle timeout and verified per-store policies with semaphores. HLD sc1/sc6 implement those choices. The existing server validates client label and pid, providing the proposed identity inputs. findings.premise: Requests currently overlap, and client identity is optional; per-session FIFO is new behavior.
findings.evidence: handleConnection starts each message with 'void this.handleMessage(trimmed, socket)' without awaiting previous messages. handleMessage dispatches handlers independently. validClient returns undefined for missing or malformed identity, without rejecting the request. [files: src/daemon/server.ts, src/shared/types.ts]
findings.action: Retain the explicit compatibility distinction between attributed FIFO and overlapping unattributed requests.

findings.premise: Detached runs retain append-only progress frames and cursor-based polling; 64 is a soft retention target with cleanup on start.
findings.evidence: startWorkflowRun inserts the run then calls gc(); progress uses state.frames.push(f). pollWorkflowRun slices frames from the cursor and returns model/result/error. gc() filters for status !== 'running', so active runs can exceed MAX_RUNS = 64. [files: src/daemon/workflow-run-registry.ts]
findings.action: Preserve these semantics in shared run storage.

findings.premise: An existing in-daemon client directly invokes handler maps and must be adapted for nested worker dispatch.
findings.evidence: createInDaemonClient accepts RpcHandlers and StreamHandlers. Its unary transport executes 'return await handler(params)'; its stream transport invokes handler(params, send, inner.signal). index.ts installs it using the same maps supplied to IpcServer. [files: src/daemon/steps/daemon-client.ts, src/daemon/index.ts]
findings.action: Reuse this transport seam, preserving its timeout, cancellation and stream-error behavior while making same-session calls inline and cross-class calls remote.

findings.premise: The proposed status-board contracts contain enough information to preserve existing daemon.status fields without store reads.
findings.evidence: sc4 stores repository snapshots as only path/completeness and unattributedUnwritable as a number. The actual response requires RegisteredRepo[], including 'name', 'addedAt', 'status', optional lastIndexed/errorMsg/lastRun, and UnattributedUnwritableCount = '{ total: number; reasons: Record<string, number> }'. buildDaemonStatus returns these structures. The proposed snapshot cannot reconstruct the promised unchanged response. [files: src/shared/types.ts, src/daemon/status.ts, src/daemon/index.ts, docs/epics/multi-threaded-daemon-sessions-admin-indexing-E2026102186197ac6/HLD.md]
findings.action: Publish complete RegisteredRepo records and the existing UnattributedUnwritableCount shape. Specify initialization/unavailability behavior that preserves required response fields.

findings.premise: Code-review state updates preserve the same token today, so a stable-token lifecycle preserves compatibility.
findings.evidence: The code-review store has saveState/loadState/releaseState but no updateState. handleStart consumes the confirm_wait token with 'releaseState(step.state!)' and later creates a fresh token using saveState. Decline and timeout paths also release the old token before beginDiffOnlyReview saves a new one. Thus the blanket stable-token policy changes token validity and replay behavior. [files: src/daemon/steps/code-review-step/state-store.ts, src/daemon/steps/code-review-step/handler.ts, docs/epics/multi-threaded-daemon-sessions-admin-indexing-E2026102186197ac6/HLD.md]
findings.action: Model code-review lifecycle by transition: consume the wait token and mint a new judgement token on resume/fallback, then consume the judgement token on completion. Test that superseded tokens fail.

findings.premise: All four existing step stores have independent 100-entry caps, one-hour idle TTLs and reads that refresh activity.
findings.evidence: Each store defines MAX_ENTRIES = 100 and TTL_MS = 60 * 60 * 1_000. loadState updates touchedAt. saveState invokes sweep(), which removes expired entries and evicts least-recently-touched entries. Expiry is swept on save, not enforced on read. [files: src/daemon/steps/analyze-step/state-store.ts, src/daemon/steps/workflow-step/state-store.ts, src/daemon/steps/review-step/state-store.ts, src/daemon/steps/code-review-step/state-store.ts]
findings.action: Preserve the separate per-kind capacities and save-triggered expiry semantics; do not silently change to strict expiration on read.

findings.premise: The five Story responsibilities and their ordering preserve the upstream Epic boundaries.
findings.evidence: DEF assigns stores to S001, classification/admin to S002, indexing to S003, session isolation to S004 and visibility to S005. Its dependency edges permit S002/S003 after S001, S004 after S001/S002, and S005 after S002/S004. HLD retains those responsibilities and adds shared-contract dependencies consistent with that order. findings.premise: The router can determine that a dead worker's native store operations have finished before reclaiming its semaphore.
findings.evidence: Read the graph transaction wrapper, Lance connection lifecycle, DuckDB connection cleanup and LMDB native environment cleanup. These expose transaction promises and library-specific cleanup, but no common router-visible native-operation completion barrier. sc1 provides reclaim(threadId) but no mechanism establishing its safety precondition. No production-launch worker-termination verification was performed. The analyzer also failed with shaper-llm-unavailable due to an invalid planner output schema. findings.premise: The existing locks-lost shutdown path skips store closure and ends the process with SIGKILL.
findings.evidence: createShutdown detects locks-lost, skips queue waiting/store closure and schedules endAfterStoreFailure. That function clears process files, writes the final diagnostic and calls killSelf; production killSelf executes process.kill(process.pid, 'SIGKILL'). Healthy shutdown separately has a 20-second hard-exit backstop. [files: src/daemon/shutdown.ts]
findings.action: Preserve both the locks-lost path and the healthy-shutdown backstop when adding worker draining.

summary.prose: The daemon's main thread becomes a router that only accepts connections and hands each request to the right worker thread: one admin worker, one indexing worker, and a pool of session workers with one worker per client session, reused while the session is active and released after it sits idle. Every worker opens the stores itself; a store proven safe across threads is used directly, and any other store is guarded by a process-wide semaphore that is always released. State that must outlive a worker, such as MCP step tokens, lives in a shared store, so releasing an idle worker loses nothing.

body.frameworkSummary: Alternative a1: a routing main thread plus worker threads by class of work. The main thread owns the Unix socket, framing and the attached-client registry, and does no handler work. Each request is classified (admin, session or indexing) and forwarded over a thread channel to its target: the admin worker, the indexing worker, or the session's pooled worker (session id = the request's client label and process id). Workers each load the handler runtime and open their own store handles under a verified per-store threading policy: direct use where a store is proven safe, a shared semaphore with guaranteed release where it is not. MCP step state (the four step state stores) moves into a store shared by all threads, so it outlives any worker; a detached workflow run stays owned by the worker that started it, which is not released while the run is active, and the run's record is published where every thread can read it. A request that carries no valid client identity is served on one shared unattributed worker, as today's daemon serves it, kept apart from every session. A shared status board lets every thread publish what it is doing, which the admin worker reads for daemon status and liveness.
body.architectureShape:
Main thread (router): accepts socket connections, parses each request, looks up the method's class in the method-class registry and the session id from the request's client envelope, and sends a request envelope over the thread channel to the target registered for that class. It writes reply and stream-frame envelopes back to the originating connection and observes worker exits, failing that worker's in-flight requests with an error and reclaiming any semaphores the worker held.

Admin worker: one long-lived worker that serves every admin-class method (ping, daemon.status, daemon.debug-status, the TUI's and daemon-ctl's reads and controls). It never runs session or indexing work.

Indexing worker: one long-lived worker hosting the index queue with both lanes and the file-watcher feed; indexing-class methods route to it, and its lane status and idle state are published on the status board so other threads read them without calling into it.

Session pool: a thread pool keyed by session id. A request whose session already has a mapped worker is queued to that worker, which runs its session's requests one at a time in arrival order; otherwise the pool creates a worker and maps it. A worker idle beyond the pool's idle timeout is released, unless it still owns an active detached workflow run; a later request from that session gets a new worker and finds its step state in the shared step-state store. Running a session's requests one at a time is new behaviour required by k1: today the server starts every request without waiting for earlier ones, so a session's requests can overlap. A call a running request makes to another method through the in-daemon client runs immediately on the same worker as part of that request, never queued behind it, so the in-order rule cannot deadlock a request on its own nested calls.

Unattributed worker: a session-class request whose client identity is missing or invalid (the identity field is optional on the wire and some clients do not send it) goes to one shared unattributed worker that serves such requests the way today's daemon does, overlapping, and never mixes them into a real session.

Detached workflow runs: a run started by workflow.run keeps its live execution (its driver and abort controller) in the worker that started it. The run's full poll state (status, the append-only sequence of progress frames, the model, and the terminal result or error) is written to shared run storage as it happens, so a poll from any thread returns the same frames-since-cursor, model, result and error it returns today, even after the owning worker has gone; only the live driver and its abort controller stay in the worker; an abort is sent to the owning worker over the thread channel; if the owning worker exits, the router marks its active runs failed. Retention stays today's: 64 is a soft target, cleanup runs when a run starts, and a running run is never evicted, so more than 64 runs can exist while they are running.

Stores: the LMDB graph environment is opened once per process and every worker uses that one environment; no worker ever closes it, so releasing or losing a worker cannot close a descriptor the process's LMDB locks depend on. Each worker opens its own handles to the other stores. Story s1 verifies each store's contract from several threads in one process (LMDB graph, each Lance table, the in-memory DuckDB pool). A store that passes is used directly; a store that does not is used only through the store guard, a process-wide counting semaphore in shared memory acquired by one helper that releases on success, throw and cancellation, and whose holder is recorded so the router can reclaim it if the holding worker exits; reclaim happens only after the dead worker's in-flight native store calls have finished, so no store call is still running when another thread takes the lock. Each store defines how that quiescence is observed (s1 verifies it per store), with a time limit: if quiescence cannot be established within it, the store is marked unhealthy and the router restarts the daemon through the shutdown path rather than let a second thread use the store. A worker holds at most one store lock at a time, so lock cycles cannot form, and an acquisition that waits past its limit fails with an error rather than hanging. A guarded operation that spans awaits keeps its lock for the whole operation, so no other thread sees it half-done. The guard serialises access; it does not make an operation atomic. Each LMDB write stays one synchronous transaction that commits all or nothing, as today, and an operation that commits LMDB and then writes Lance keeps today's order and today's recovery (a re-embed backfills vectors whose write failed after the commit).

Admin status reads never touch a store: everything daemon.status and repo.list report that comes from a store today (the full registered-repository records with each repository's index completeness, and the daemon-wide unattributed-entity count with its reasons) is published on the status board by the indexing worker after each change, in exactly today's response shapes, and those methods read only the board. Until a value has been published the response keeps every field and marks the value unavailable instead of waiting. Admin methods that genuinely need a store (repo.stats, daemon.backup, daemon.compact) may take the store guard, but a guard wait is always asynchronous, never a blocking wait, so the admin worker keeps answering ping and status while one of them waits.

Cross-class calls inside a handler (a session handler waiting for indexing to go idle, or the in-daemon step client calling another method) go through the thread channel to the method's class target instead of calling a local copy of the handler.

Shutdown: the router coordinates it. An admin request to stop (daemon.shutdown, daemon-ctl stop) asks the router, which stops accepting connections, drains the index queue and the workers, closes the stores and exits, as today's shutdown does. Store health is shared across threads: when any thread finds the LMDB locks lost, the router takes today's locks-lost path, skipping store closure and sending SIGKILL to the process.

sharedContracts.name: Store guard and per-store threading policy
sharedContracts.purpose: Lets any thread use a store safely: records, per store, whether it is used directly or through a semaphore, and gives one helper that acquires and always releases the store's semaphore. Waiting for a lock is always asynchronous, so a waiting thread keeps serving its other work.

sharedContracts.name: Shared step-state store
sharedContracts.purpose: Keeps MCP step tokens where every thread can read them, so a session served by a new worker after an idle release, or after its worker failed, resumes its step exactly as today. Each of the four step kinds keeps its own lifecycle through an adapter: a 100-entry least-recently-used cap, a read that refreshes the token's expiry, a 1-hour idle TTL, analyze and workflow updates that mint a new token and release the old one, review updates that keep the same token, and code-review transitions that consume the current token and mint a new one at each stage (wait → judgement, fallback), so a superseded token fails exactly as today.

sharedContracts.name: Thread channel and target registry
sharedContracts.purpose: The one message contract between the router and every worker: request, reply, stream frame, cancel and error envelopes, plus the registry where a worker registers as the target for a class of work. A session-class request with no valid session id resolves to the unattributed target.

sharedContracts.name: Thread status board
sharedContracts.purpose: Shared record each thread updates as it starts and finishes work: the router publishes its attached-client snapshot, the indexing worker publishes lane state, summary-sweep progress, each repository's completeness and the unattributed-entity count, and detached workflow runs publish their full poll state, so the admin thread can answer status, debug-status, liveness and run polls without calling into a busy thread or touching a store.

sharedContracts.name: Method-class registry
sharedContracts.purpose: Declares the class of every RPC and stream method the daemon serves, so the router sends each request to the right kind of thread and no method is left unclassified.

sharedContracts.name: Session pool
sharedContracts.purpose: Maps each session id to its worker, creating one on first need, queuing a session's requests to it in arrival order, running a request's nested calls inline, and releasing a worker after its idle timeout unless it owns an active detached run.

storyBoundaries.internal: Verifying each store from several threads of one process (the LMDB graph environment, every Lance table, the in-memory DuckDB pool), including that a worker opening and later releasing its handles does not close a descriptor the process's locks depend on; the semaphore implementation over process-wide shared memory and its holder record; moving the four in-memory step state stores onto the shared step-state store with today's TTL; the status board's attached-client, sweep-progress and run-record slots; the thread channel's serialisation and the target registry's bookkeeping; the status board's shared-memory layout. As the root Story it owns every cross-cutting contract the other Stories consume. Validation: ac1 — one thread writes a repo's entities while another reads the same graph, the reader sees only whole transactions, and an entity's vectors are written only after its graph commit; ac2 — two threads write different artifacts or config entries and a third thread reads both back; ac3 — no code path outside the daemon opens a store; ac4 — a throwing LMDB transaction on one thread leaves nothing visible to another. Also: a worker opening and releasing its handles keeps the process's LMDB locks; the guard releases on success, throw, cancel and worker kill; an acquisition past its limit fails; nested acquisition is refused. Step-state compatibility: for each of the four kinds, token rotation (analyze, workflow), stable-token update (review) or consume-and-mint per stage (code-review, where a superseded token fails), read refresh of expiry, the 100-entry eviction and a missing-token error behave as today. LMDB is opened once per process and never closed by a worker; lock reclaim waits for a dead worker's in-flight native calls. Per store, a quiescence observation with a time limit and an unhealthy-store outcome when it is exceeded; a guard wait never blocks its thread.

The main-thread router (connection handling, classification, envelope forwarding, writing replies and frames back, observing worker exits, reclaiming a dead worker's store locks, coordinating shutdown and the locks-lost path), starting and supervising the admin worker, and classifying all 189 methods. Until a class's target is registered (before s3 or s4 lands) the router serves that class on a fallback worker, so each Story can ship alone. Validation: ac1 and ac2 — ping and daemon.status answer within 100 ms while a session worker spins the CPU and while an indexing pass runs, including while another worker holds the graph guard; ac3 — each admin method's response matches today's recorded response; ac4 — a test enumerates every served RPC and stream method and fails on any without a class, and a dispatch test sends each admin-class method and asserts it ran on the admin thread. Also: debug-status keeps every field including lastMethod; daemon.status and repo.list read only the status board and keep today's full response shapes (RegisteredRepo records, the unattributed count with reasons); contention tests show ping, daemon.status, repo.list and the TUI's other admin reads answer within 100 ms while an indexing pass runs and another worker holds the graph guard, including while repo.stats waits on the guard on the admin worker; shutdown and the locks-lost path behave as today.

Hosting the index queue, both lanes and the file-watcher feed in one indexing worker that registers as the indexing-class target, keeping today's lane ordering and summary-lane yielding, and publishing lane state, idleness, summary-sweep progress, the full registered-repository records with each repository's completeness, and the unattributed-entity count with its reasons, on the status board after every change. Validation: ac1 — a session request is answered during an indexing pass; ac2 — a file change is indexed while a session worker is busy; ac3 — lane order and indexed results equal the single-thread baseline for the same input; ac4 — queue status and idle waiting read from another thread reflect the indexing worker's real state.

The session pool: session-id mapping, per-session FIFO, worker creation and idle release, containment of a failing worker (its in-flight requests fail with an error, the next request gets a new worker), routing each step handler's state through the shared step-state store, the unattributed worker, inline nested calls, and ownership of detached workflow runs (records on the status board, abort routed to the owner, failure on owner exit, never idle-released while a run is active). Validation: ac1 — session B is answered while session A's worker spins; ac2 — A's second request starts only after its first completes; ac3 — requests from one client process over separate connections run on one worker, released after the idle timeout; ac4 — a worker failure fails only its session's requests; ac5 — provider calls stay serial (no Promise.all reaching a provider); ac6 — a step token minted before an idle release resumes on the new worker. Also: unattributed requests are served apart from sessions; a nested in-daemon call completes without deadlock; a detached run survives idle time, accepts an abort from another thread, and is marked failed when its owner exits; a poll from another thread, and after the owner has gone, returns the same frames-since-cursor, model, result and error as today.

Adding a `threads` section to daemon.status and daemon.debug-status from the status board and session pool (additive fields only), and making the liveness answer report a busy session as busy rather than as a failure. Validation: ac1 — daemon.status lists each thread with class, session, busy state, method and elapsed time; ac2 — with a session worker busy for minutes the liveness answer reports the daemon alive and the session busy; ac3 — every field of today's daemon.status and daemon.debug-status, including clients and sweep progress, is present with the same meaning.

nonFunctional.performance: Ping and daemon.status answer within 100 ms at the 99th percentile while a session worker is CPU-bound and while an indexing pass runs; routing adds no more than 5 ms per request and per stream frame. A session worker's idle timeout defaults to 15 minutes and is configurable; step state keeps its own 1-hour TTL independent of worker release.
nonFunctional.security: No new listener or socket: the main thread keeps the existing Unix socket and its permissions; shared memory and thread channels are internal to the daemon process; clients still reach the stores only through IPC.
nonFunctional.observability: Every log line carries its thread id and class, and the session id for session work; daemon.status lists every thread with class, session, busy state, current method and elapsed time; a store-lock wait beyond its acquisition limit and a reclaimed lock after a worker exit are logged as warnings.
nonFunctional.durability: Step state survives a worker's release or failure because it lives in the shared step-state store; a detached workflow run lives in its owning worker, which is not released while the run is active, and is marked failed if that worker exits; its poll state lives in shared run storage, so polls still answer after the owner has gone. A worker that exits while holding a store lock has the lock reclaimed by the router. Atomicity is unchanged from today: each LMDB write transaction commits all or nothing, and an operation that writes LMDB then Lance keeps today's order and re-embed recovery. The LMDB environment is opened once per process and closed only by the router at shutdown; a lock held by a dead worker is reclaimed only after its in-flight native calls have finished.

phases.name: Phase A — store safety and shared contracts
phases.rationale: Every other Story consumes sc1-sc4, which s1 owns; and no work may move off the main thread until each store's behaviour from several threads is verified and the step state lives where any thread can read it.
phases.backwardCompat: The daemon still runs single-threaded in this phase: the store guard, shared step-state store, channel and status board are exercised by tests and used in place of today's in-memory step maps, so step tokens keep their 1-hour TTL and every existing response is unchanged.

phases.name: Phase B — router, admin worker and indexing worker
phases.rationale: s2 and s3 each depend only on s1 and can land in either order: s2 puts the router and admin worker in front of every request and classifies all methods, and s3 moves the index queue to its own worker and registers it as the indexing target.
phases.backwardCompat: Methods whose class has no registered worker yet are served on the router's fallback worker exactly as today, so session work keeps running unchanged until Phase C; IPC method names, request shapes and response fields are untouched.

phases.name: Phase C — session pool
phases.rationale: s4 consumes sc5 from s2 and sc2 from s1, so it follows Phase B; it moves session work onto per-session workers with idle release.
phases.backwardCompat: Step tokens minted before the switch remain valid because they already live in the shared step-state store from Phase A. Running a session's requests one at a time in arrival order is new behaviour (today they can overlap); nested in-daemon calls from a running request run inline on the same worker, and requests without a valid client identity keep today's overlapping behaviour on the unattributed worker.

phases.name: Phase D — thread visibility
phases.rationale: s5 reads the status board and the session pool (sc6), so it lands after s4.
phases.backwardCompat: daemon.status and daemon.debug-status only gain a threads section; every existing field keeps its name and meaning for the TUI and both plugins.

rolloutOverview.orderingRationale: The order follows the Epic's dependsOn edges and contract ownership: s1 owns sc1-sc4 consumed by all others, s2 owns sc5 consumed by s4 and s5, and s4 owns sc6 consumed by s5. s2 and s3 share Phase B because both depend only on s1. One flag (daemon.threads.enabled) gates the move of work off the main thread in Phases B and C, so the single-thread path stays available until the threaded daemon has run live.

riskyBits.why: This daemon has already lost its LMDB locks when another descriptor on the lock file closed; a worker that opens the environment and later closes it on idle release could drop the process's locks for every thread.
riskyBits.mitigation: s1 reproduces open-and-release from a worker against the production launch before anything else and keeps every worker on one process-wide environment that is never closed by a worker; until that test passes, LMDB is guarded and opened once.

riskyBits.area: Module-scope state that silently splits per worker
riskyBits.why: Beyond the step stores, caches and registries are module-scope (template caches, the run-record map, the repository-map cache, the chat session pool); a handler that relied on one shared copy would silently see a per-worker copy.
riskyBits.mitigation: s1 inventories every module-scope mutable value in code reachable from a handler and classifies each as per-thread-safe, moved to a shared store, or owned by one class's worker; s2's classification refuses a method whose state is unclassified.

riskyBits.area: Lock leaks and deadlocks in the store guard
riskyBits.why: A guarded operation that throws, is cancelled, or whose worker dies while holding the semaphore would block every other thread; a thread taking two locks could deadlock.
riskyBits.mitigation: One acquire-and-release helper is the only way to take a lock; it releases in every exit path, records its holder for router reclaim on worker exit, fails an acquisition past its limit with an error, and forbids nested acquisition, each covered by a test that kills or throws inside the guarded operation.

riskyBits.why: Step handlers call other daemon methods through the in-daemon client; if such a call queued behind the request that made it, the request would wait on itself forever.
riskyBits.mitigation: A nested call made from a running request executes inline on the same worker as part of that request and is never queued; s4 covers it with a test where a step handler's nested call completes.

alternativesConsidered.name: Router on the main thread; admin, indexing and session work all in worker threads
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The main thread only accepts connections and routes each request to a dedicated admin worker, the indexing worker or the session's pooled worker; every worker runs the handler runtime and opens its own store handles, with shared semaphores guarding stores that are not thread-safe.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
The main thread keeps the Unix socket and the per-connection framing and does nothing else: it reads each request's method and client identity, classifies the method as admin, session or indexing work, and forwards it to the right worker. Admin work goes to one dedicated admin worker, index-queue work to one indexing worker, and session work to a thread pool keyed by session id that reuses the session's mapped worker or creates one, and releases a worker after an idle timeout. Replies and stream frames come back to the main thread, which writes them to the originating connection.

Every worker loads the handler runtime and opens its own handles to the stores. Each store is used directly where its threading contract is verified safe, and otherwise behind a semaphore shared by all workers (process-wide shared memory), acquired and released through one helper that releases on every exit path. Session state that must outlive a worker (MCP step state, the workflow run registry) moves out of worker module memory into a shared place every worker can read, so an idle-released or failed worker loses nothing.
pros: The main thread does no handler work at all, so no handler of any class can delay accepting or routing a request.
Admin work cannot be delayed by routing load either: it has its own worker, satisfying k2 literally.
A crash in any worker is contained: the main thread observes the worker exit and fails only that worker's in-flight requests.
cons: Every request crosses a thread boundary twice (route in, reply out), adding a message hop per request and per stream frame.
Four kinds of thread to start, supervise and shut down (main, admin, indexing, session pool), the most moving parts of the alternatives.
Every worker re-imports the handler runtime and re-opens store handles, multiplying start-up cost and open handles by the worker count.

alternativesConsidered.name: Store-owner main thread; workers proxy every store call to it
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Workers run admin, indexing and session logic, but the stores stay open only on the main thread and every store call from a worker becomes a message to it.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
Admin, indexing and session work move to worker threads as in the stakeholder's model, but no worker opens a store. The main thread keeps the single existing store handles and serves store operations as messages: a worker that reads the graph, writes an artifact or queries a table sends the operation to the main thread and awaits the result.

Consistency comes from serialising all store work on one thread, so no store needs a semaphore and no worker-level store threading contract has to be verified. Session state can stay on the main thread beside the stores.
pros: No store is ever opened twice in the process, so no per-store threading contract has to be verified.
Session state and store handles stay where they are today, so the smallest share of existing module-scope state moves.
cons: All store access from every session and the indexer is serialised on one thread: a heavy indexing write pass delays every session's reads, the cross-session stall the Epic removes, for store-bound work.
Every graph traversal becomes a message per store call; analyzer recipes that make hundreds of graph reads per request pay a thread hop on each.
It is the owner-thread model the stakeholder declined in favour of semaphores for stores that are not thread-safe.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Strongest on k7 but only partial on k1, k2 and k3, because the store-owner thread re-couples every class of work; it is also the owner-thread model the stakeholder declined.

alternativesConsidered.name: Main thread doubles as router and admin thread; indexing and sessions in workers
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The main thread accepts connections, routes, and itself serves the admin class; indexing and session work run in workers that open their own store handles behind shared semaphores where needed.
alternativesConsidered.approach:
The main thread keeps the socket and routes requests as in a1, but instead of forwarding admin requests it runs the admin handlers itself, making the main thread the one admin thread. Session work goes to the session-keyed worker pool with idle release, and index-queue work to the one indexing worker.

The main thread must therefore stay free of long work: only handlers verified to be short and bounded may be classed as admin. Store use and shared session state are handled as in a1: verified-safe stores used directly, the rest behind shared semaphores with guaranteed release, and session state that must outlive a worker kept outside worker memory.
pros: Admin requests are answered without any thread hop, the lowest-latency path for ping and status.
One fewer thread kind to supervise than a1.
cons: Routing and admin share one thread: a mis-classified slow admin handler blocks routing for every client, recreating today's freeze for the whole daemon.
Admin handlers that read the stores (daemon.status reads the repository list) put store access, and any semaphore wait, on the routing thread.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Matches a1 except on k2, where sharing routing with admin work puts any store wait of an admin handler on the thread every client depends on.
